analysis.one_liner: Cuts off federal energy money to utilities that raise home electricity rates.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee since its referral with no action and just one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar the Energy Department from giving financial assistance to regulated investor-owned electric utilities that raise residential electricity rates above their January 1, 2026 level. For the first year, any rate increase means no federal money. For the next two years, a utility could keep federal aid despite raising rates only if it cuts the pay of its five highest-paid executives by twice the size of the rate increase and reports the numbers to the Department.
analysis.who_benefits: Households that pay residential electric bills. If a utility wants to raise rates and still receive federal assistance, it must first absorb the increase by cutting the pay of its five highest-compensated executives, so ratepayers are not the only ones paying for higher bills.

how_it_helps.text: For one year after enactment, the Energy Secretary may not provide financial assistance to any regulated investor-owned utility that charges residential customers more than its January 1, 2026 rate [S2].
A utility receiving federal assistance that raises residential rates above the January 1, 2026 level during that first year must have the assistance terminated [S2].

In the following two years, a utility that raises rates above the January 2026 level can only keep federal assistance if it does not increase the total compensation of its five highest-paid employees, cuts that compensation by twice the percentage-point rate increase at the time of the increase, and files a report documenting both figures with the Secretary [S2].
The bill defines total compensation broadly to include salary, bonuses, stock awards, stock options, and any other financial remuneration, so executives cannot shield pay through equity awards [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Investor-owned electric utilities lose access to Department of Energy financial assistance if they raise residential rates, and their top executives face pay cuts as the price of keeping that assistance during years two and three. Consumers still bear any rate increases a utility chooses to make, since the bill penalizes rate hikes rather than blocking them outright.
analysis.who_pays_short: Investor-owned utilities and their top executives

drawbacks.text: The bill does not cap rates directly; it only conditions federal financial assistance, so a utility that raises rates and does not need or receive Energy Department aid faces no penalty at all [S2].

Freezing rates at their January 1, 2026 level ignores real cost drivers, such as fuel prices, grid upgrades, and growing electricity demand, and could discourage utilities from accepting federal assistance or push costs onto commercial and industrial customers instead [S2].

The executive-pay offset formula is mechanical: reducing the pay of five executives by twice a small percentage-point rate increase would offset only a tiny fraction of the extra revenue a rate increase produces [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core idea—tying federal dollars to ratepayer protection—is straightforward and gives utilities a clear choice between raising rates and keeping federal aid. But its coverage is narrow: it only binds utilities that take Energy Department money, and the executive-pay offsets in years two and three are largely symbolic relative to the revenue a rate increase generates. It is a targeted lever on utilities' behavior, not a broad rate cap.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and has sat there since, with no markup, no vote, and only one cosponsor.

narrative.text: Representative Haley Stevens introduced the bill on March 12, 2026, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1].
No further action has been taken: no committee markup, no floor vote, and no additional steps appear in the action history [S4].
The bill has one cosponsor, a House Democrat, in addition to its sponsor [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: As things stand, investor-owned utilities and their executives are better off: they remain free to raise residential rates and set executive pay without risking federal financial assistance, while households continue to face rising electric bills with no new protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Utilities and their executives, for now

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat introduced the bill with one Democratic cosponsor and no Republican support; no votes have been recorded, so the partisan shape is not yet established.

industries.note: Utilities that raise residential rates above their January 2026 level would forfeit Energy Department financial assistance. The industry's interest in keeping both federal aid and the freedom to raise rates runs against ratepayers' interest in stable bills.

industries.industry: Utility executives (top-5 compensated at assisted utilities)
industries.note: Executives at utilities seeking federal aid despite a rate increase would face mandatory compensation cuts of twice the rate increase. The cost of a rate hike would shift from customers partly onto executive pay.

analysis.trajectory: With one cosponsor and no committee movement since referral, the bill is unlikely to advance. Single-sponsor energy bills that sit in committee without a markup almost never reach the floor; it will most likely die at the end of this Congress unless it gains substantial cosponsors or a committee vehicle to attach to.
